about.title: About
about.intro:
Project Cherenkov is an open-source archive of interactive olympiad editorials for informatics, physics and astronomy. Each editorial explains one idea in full: a proof or derivation, and a visualization you can manipulate. Editorials are filed by the mistake they correct, not by syllabus chapter.

Around the archive sit a syllabus and short materials, for browsing by topic, and a study planner with a companion called Neutrino. The syllabus and the planner follow the Indonesian OSN today.
about.whyText: Why it looks and sounds like this and documentations:
about.repoBody: Cherenkov is built in the open. Every editorial is a git-tracked file, so the commit history is public. Contribute on GitHub.
about.metaDescription: Project Cherenkov is an open-source archive of interactive olympiad editorials for informatics, physics and astronomy, with an OSN syllabus and study planner.

what-is.a: An archive of editorials and a study planner for the Indonesian science olympiad (OSN), covering informatics, physics and astronomy. Each editorial explains one idea in full, such as a proof, a derivation or a technique, and comes with an interactive visualization that you can change and step through.

account-needed.a:
No. You can read everything without one: the syllabus, materials, editorials, visualizations, search, the timer and this FAQ.

An account is needed for the study planner, topic quizzes, saving finished timer sessions, your progress pages and AI chat.

three-sections.q: What is the difference between the syllabus, materials and editorials?
three-sections.a:
The syllabus lists the official OSN scope for each subject, topic by topic, and shows which topics already have a material or editorials.

Materials are short breakdowns of single syllabus topics, good for quick revision.

Editorials are the archive proper: one idea written out in full, with a working visualization and the complete proof.

where-begin.a: If you want to know what you are expected to learn, open the syllabus and pick your subject. If you made a specific mistake or want to know why something is true, use the filters in the archive, which are organised by principle and error type rather than by chapter. If you only need a quick refresher on one topic, look for its material.

subjects-coverage.q: Which subjects are covered, and is everything written yet?
subjects-coverage.a: The syllabus covers informatics, physics and astronomy. The site is still growing, so not every syllabus topic has a material or an editorial yet; the syllabus shows which ones do. Quiz questions are uneven too: physics has the most, and informatics and astronomy have fewer, so some of their topics cannot be confirmed by quiz yet.

language.a: Yes. Use the ID / EN control in the header to switch the interface between Indonesian and English. Each editorial and material is written in one language and appears as written in both interfaces. Some documentation pages are currently available in English only.

search.q: How do I search the site?
search.a: Press Ctrl+K (Cmd+K on a Mac) or use the search button in the header. It searches editorials, materials, syllabus topics and the documentation. Searching happens in your browser, so what you type is not sent to a server.

phone.q: Does it work on a phone?
phone.a: Yes. Nothing on the site depends on hover, and the visualization controls work by touch or keyboard. On narrow screens (under 640 px wide) Neutrino opens as a bottom sheet instead of a floating panel.

anatomy.a:
It opens with a hook, one sentence on what is surprising, then the problem and the idea: the key insight, stated before any heavy algebra. Next comes the interactive visualization under “Try it”, then the full proof with every step written out, and finally tags for finding related editorials. The visualization sits before the proof on purpose, so you see the claim before you read the argument for it.

Formulas are typeset with KaTeX and also provided as accessible MathML for screen readers.

principle-error.a: Both appear near the top of every editorial. The principle is the general idea it teaches, one that applies beyond the single problem. The error type is the specific mistake it corrects, when there is one. The archive filters use them, so following a principle from one editorial to the next is a good way to find more on the same idea.

try-first.a: On editorials that keep their proof in a solution block, turning on “Try it first” collapses the solution behind a “Show solution” control so you can attempt the problem yourself. It is off by default, and the setting is kept only in your browser.

viz-controls.q: How do I use a visualization?
viz-controls.a:
Most share one control bar: step back and forward, play and pause, reset, and a slider to jump to any step or moment. Nothing plays until you press Play. Sandbox-style visualizations also have sliders for their key quantities, such as launch angle or orbital eccentricity.

Everything works by keyboard. Tab moves between controls, Space or Enter presses a button, and on a slider the arrow keys change the value by one step, Page Up and Page Down by a larger step, and Home and End jump to the ends.

viz-broken.q: A visualization does not load. What should I do?
viz-broken.a: Visualizations load after the page, so you may see a placeholder for a moment. They need JavaScript, but the text of the editorial, including the full proof, is available without it. If one shows a configuration error, the editorial’s setup is at fault rather than your browser, so please report it with the page address and what you did just before.

syllabus-link.q: How do the syllabus and the editorials connect?
syllabus-link.a: An editorial or material can be linked to a syllabus topic. When it is, its page links back to that topic, and the topic’s row in the syllabus links forward to it. Use the syllabus as the table of contents and the editorials as the deep dives.

planner-what.q: What does the study planner do?
planner-what.a: It builds an adaptive revision schedule for the OSN stages: regency/city (OSN-K), province (OSN-P), and the national semifinal and final. It assumes you already know a lot and tries to spend your time where it should help most. You need an account to use it.

planner-setup.q: How do I set up my plan?
planner-setup.a: The first time you open the planner it asks for your subject, the stage you are aiming for, your exam year, your weekly study hours and your time zone (Asia/Jakarta by default). Then you rate each syllabus topic from 1 (“barely know it”) to 5 (“could teach it”). A topic you leave unrated counts as “no opinion”. You can change any of this later from the dashboard.

planner-confirm.q: Why does my plan start with quizzes?
planner-confirm.a: A self-rating is a weak signal, so the planner asks you to confirm what you say you know. Topics you rated high are quizzed first, so an over-confident guess is caught early; topics you rated low are confirmed last. Quiz answers then update the planner’s estimate of what you know, and that estimate fades slowly with time to allow for forgetting.

planner-contents.a: After the confirmation quizzes, the plan holds study sessions ranked by how much you are likely to gain per hour, spaced reviews timed backwards from your exam date, and a buffer before the exam with a final mixed pass. Each day mixes several topics instead of one long block, and every item says why it is there. The dashboard shows today’s tasks, anything overdue, what is coming next and the weeks ahead.

planner-short.q: What if my weekly hours are not enough?
planner-short.a: The dashboard shows a banner with the shortfall, the topics that did not fit and any review sessions that were skipped. You can raise your weekly hours or change your target, then regenerate the plan.

planner-regen.q: Does regenerating the plan erase my progress?
planner-regen.a: No. Regenerating keeps the items you have already completed and never reschedules finished study. It only happens when you ask for it, and a banner tells you when your settings or quiz answers have changed since the plan was made. “Today” follows the time zone in your settings, not the server’s.

planner-quiz.q: How do the topic quizzes work?
planner-quiz.a: Each topic page in the planner has a multiple-choice quiz. The difficulty follows your target stage: basic to intermediate questions for OSN-K, intermediate to advanced for OSN-P, and advanced for the semifinal and final. Correct answers are not sent to your browser before you submit. Passing a topic’s quiz completes its confirmation item in your plan automatically.

planner-trust.q: How much should I trust the plan?
planner-trust.a: Treat it as a reasoned guide, not a guarantee. The target mastery levels have not yet been calibrated on real students, and exam dates for 2027 are projected from 2026 rather than announced. The plan also only knows what you tell it and what quizzes measure, and some subjects have few quiz questions so far.

timer-how.q: How does the study timer work?
timer-how.a: Pick a preset (25 minutes of focus with a 5-minute break, 50/10 or 90/5) or set your own lengths: focus from 1 to 180 minutes and breaks from 1 to 60. Run it in Neutrino’s Timer tab or on the Timer page. Both share one timer, so a running timer shows in either place, and because it keeps its state in your browser a reload does not lose it.

timer-count.a: Only focus time. Breaks are never logged. Time is worked out from timestamps rather than by counting ticks, so a sleeping laptop or a background tab cannot inflate it: if the machine sleeps through a block, that block is credited at most its planned length.

timer-save.q: Why was my session not saved?
timer-save.a: A finished session is saved only when you are signed in and press “Finish and save”. The server also checks that it lasted at least a minute and at most 12 hours, is not in the future, and does not overlap another session. You can also log time you studied away from the timer by hand.

progress-page.q: What does the Progress page show?
progress-page.a: This week’s active days, minutes per day, time by topic and a map of syllabus coverage. A day counts as active when you logged at least 10 minutes or took a quiz; opening the site does not count and there are no streaks. The map keeps “not enough data” separate from “not known yet” and shows how many answers each estimate rests on. It is private to you.

missed-questions.q: Where do I find the questions I got wrong?
missed-questions.a: On the Missed questions page, which you can filter by subject, topic, status and how recently you missed them. You can retry a question or ask to see its answer. A retry is practice only: it can resolve a miss but never changes your mastery estimate or your plan.

neutrino-what.a: Neutrino is the small glowing lattice that floats on every page. Click it to open a panel with three tabs: Ask, where you can use this FAQ or AI chat; Timer, the study timer; and Settings. You can drag it anywhere, resize its panel, hide it, and rename it if you are signed in.

faq-vs-ai.q: What is the difference between the FAQ and AI chat?
faq-vs-ai.a:
The FAQ opens first every time. Its answers were written by the Cherenkov team, they point to the right page, and nothing you do there is sent to an AI. It works without an account but can only answer the questions it lists.

AI chat answers free-form study questions with replies generated by Google’s Gemini. It needs an account, counts against a daily limit and can be wrong. Use the FAQ and AI chat buttons at the top of the Ask tab to switch; the notice under them always says which one you are in.

ai-trust.q: Can I trust the AI’s answers?
ai-trust.a: Treat them as a hint, not an authority. Neutrino is told to prefer hints, explanations and checking your reasoning over unexplained answers, and to say when it is unsure, but a language model can still be confidently wrong, especially on exact numbers, proofs and olympiad problems. It cannot see the page you are reading or your plan, and it does not know Cherenkov’s content unless you type it in. Check anything that matters against an editorial, a material or your teacher.

ai-limits.q: How many AI messages can I send?
ai-limits.a: Up to {limit} requests per account per day, counted by UTC day, so the count resets at midnight UTC (07:00 in Jakarta). A failed request and a retry each count. A message can be up to {chars} characters, only your latest {history} messages are sent along, and replies are kept short. Google’s own quotas apply separately, so the AI can be unavailable even when you have requests left.

ai-privacy.q: What happens to what I type in AI chat?
ai-privacy.a: Your messages go from your browser to Cherenkov’s server and on to Google’s Gemini service, which handles them under Google’s own terms and may keep them for a limited time. Cherenkov does not store them beyond the conversation open in your browser. Do not type passwords or personal information. If you are under 18, use AI chat only with a parent’s or guardian’s knowledge and permission. The FAQ never sends anything to an AI.

ai-key.q: What is the “use my own Gemini key” option?
ai-key.a: After a quota, availability or server-configuration error, Neutrino may offer to retry once with your own Gemini API key. It is entirely optional. The key is sent to Cherenkov’s server and to Google for that one request, is not saved, and the field is cleared afterwards. It does not raise the daily limit, and you should only enter a key you control.

ai-off.q: Can I turn off the AI but keep Neutrino?
ai-off.a:
Yes. In Settings (or on your Account page) switch off “Use AI chat”. The AI chat button disappears, nothing can be sent to an AI, and the mascot, FAQ and timer carry on as before. Switch it back on whenever you like. The choice is saved to your account when you are signed in, and on this device otherwise.

To remove Neutrino altogether, turn off “Show the companion” in Settings (this needs an account). The × on the mascot only hides it until you reload the page.

neutrino-settings.q: What can I change in Neutrino’s settings?
neutrino-settings.a: Open the Settings tab, or go to your Account page; both change the same settings. You can choose the mascot’s size (small, medium or large) and how it turns (Automatic, 3D or Simple), and switch AI chat on or off, which is saved on this device when you are signed out. When you are signed in you can also rename it (1 to 32 characters) and turn the whole companion off. If your system asks for reduced motion, the mascot stays still.

neutrino-move.q: How do I move or hide Neutrino?
neutrino-move.a: Drag it anywhere on the page. With the keyboard, focus it and use the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger steps); Enter opens it. The position is remembered on this device, and “Reset position” in Settings puts it back in the bottom-right corner. The small × that appears when you hover over or focus it hides it until you reload the page.

neutrino-resize.q: Can I make the panel bigger or smaller?
neutrino-resize.a: Yes, on screens at least 640 px wide. The panel stays attached to the mascot, so you drag the two edges that face away from it, or the corner between them, which shows a small grip. Drag in either direction; the panel will not shrink below a usable minimum or leave the screen. With the keyboard, focus an edge and press the arrow keys (hold Shift for bigger steps). Double-click an edge or use “Reset panel size” in Settings to go back to the default. The size is remembered on this device.

neutrino-float.q: Can I open Neutrino in its own window?
neutrino-float.a: In a recent desktop version of Chrome, yes: choose Float in the panel’s header to open it in a separate window that stays above your other windows, which is handy for keeping the timer in view. It uses Chrome’s Document Picture-in-Picture feature, so keep the Cherenkov tab open. In other browsers use the in-page panel, which has everything the floating window has.

faq-miss.q: My question is not here. What now?
faq-miss.a: Try different words in the search box, since it looks in the answers as well as the questions. If you are signed in, switch to AI chat for a free-form study question. For how the site works, the documentation goes deeper than this FAQ, and the footer has the team’s contact details.

data-stored.q: What data does Cherenkov keep about me?
data-stored.a:
Without an account, nothing beyond the ordinary server logs kept by the hosting provider. The timer, “Try it first”, search, and Neutrino’s position and panel size all stay in your browser.

With an account it stores your email address, your sign-in details (passwords are stored hashed; with Google sign-in, your Google name and email) and the study data you create: quiz answers and retries, study sessions, pages you marked as understood, and your planner settings and ratings. It sets only the cookies needed for sign-in, language and theme, with no advertising or tracking cookies.

data-delete.a: You can delete individual study sessions on the Progress page. To delete your account, or to ask for access to or correction of your data, email the project; the address is on the Privacy page and in the footer. Chat messages are not kept by Cherenkov beyond the conversation open in your browser.

roles.a: They are the two account roles shown on your Account page. Inchoatus is the standard signed-in member: you can use the planner, quizzes and tools but cannot edit site content. Primus Inter Pares can author and edit content in the site’s editing tools, and is given to accounts whose email is on the project’s editor list.

password.q: How do I change or reset my password?
password.a: While signed in, use the password section of your Account page: it lets you change your password, or set one if you signed up with Google. If you forgot it, the sign-in page has a “Forgot password?” link that emails you a reset link. That link only appears when the site’s email service is set up, so if you do not see it, contact the team.

report.q: How do I report a mistake or a bug?
report.a: Open an issue on the project’s GitHub page or email the team, saying which page and what is wrong. For a visualization that misbehaves, include the page address, your browser and device, and what you did just before. The repository link and contact address are in the footer and on the About page.

accessibility.a: Please report it: accessibility reports are treated as bugs. Say what you were using (a screen reader, keyboard only, zoom, a switch device) and what got in the way, so it can be reproduced.

contribute.a: Yes. The project is open source under the MIT licence and every editorial is a git-tracked file. You can write an editorial or a material as an .mdx file in a pull request, translate documentation pages or interface strings, or contribute code. The contributing guide explains each route.
